before: Intentional, meaning you pick one of those acts and decide when you'll do it, and what the smallest first step is (like with the envelope). Some of them are only one step anyway. If it needs money or somebody's help, sort that out before the day, and if you'll have to tell someone something they won't like, say it out loud to yourself ahead of time. At first it'll probably come out sounding like a question.
after: (The next section, "Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust", begins: Sometimes love is available and still feels unsafe because love and trust have become tied together as though one has to validate the other. They don’t.… It isn't humanized yet.)
brief:
- Second half of guide paragraph 4: afterward, look at what actually happened. Didn't do it -> could have been fear, not being sure what you were going for, not knowing how, exhaustion, something practical; look before deciding which. Did it and didn't feel better right away -> not failure. Doing it doesn't prove it helped either. Keep and adjust the acts by what they actually add (safer, closer, more capable, more enjoyable), not by whether they earn a tick.
Note: the paragraph before is about planning one act (when, the smallest first step, what it needs, saying it out loud to yourself first). This one is after the day.
The article already asks, in an earlier section: "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" A callback can carry "doing it doesn't prove it helped" and the tick point without explaining them again.
The section's first paragraph says the underlying reason people stay in unsafe relationships is a lack of self-love, which the author holds is under all the other reasons (see his ruling). Keep this paragraph consistent with that: the reasons here are what got in the way this time, worth looking at, not a rival explanation. Don't bring self-love up again.
Your first sentence will be read together with the last lines of the paragraph before.
Limits: don't invent facts about the author's life; never call the inner child "the kid"; don't reuse the article's examples (the envelope, the boundary, the clean room, the keys, sarcasm, the old food, the angry text).
length: three to five sentences, 50 to 100 words
guide_passage: Afterward, review what actually happened. Not doing it may reflect fear, uncertainty about the goal, lack of skill, exhaustion, or a practical barrier; don’t decide which without looking. Completing it without immediate relief is not automatically failure, and completion alone does not prove it helped. Adjust the action to what it actually contributes to safety, connection, competence, or enjoyment—not just to whether it earns a tick.

rulings:
Joel, 2026-09-29, on P3: "you were conflating protection from nurturing (giving a meal is nurturing, throwing away moldy food is protection, and we already have that in P1). So I threw away the duplicated examples of protection."
Joel, 2026-09-29, on P1's self-love sentence: "lack of self love isn't the only reason to stay in an unsafe relationship, but it is the underlying reason. if you lack self love, all the others will follow: uncertainty about your goals, lack of skill follows that uncertainty, exhaustion follows that uncertainty and the lack of skill, practical barriers are less actual barriers when the goal is understood to be self love"
Joel, 2026-09-29, on logic: "the logic should be grounded in the meaning the reader needs to understand" (a flat "shows" where the guide says "can be" was pedantic to flag).
Joel, 2026-09-29, on P3: "line it up better with the guide" (one guide paragraph's job per paragraph; this paragraph is the first half of guide paragraph 4, split at its natural break because Joel breaks paragraphs at two beats).
